captions.text: Let's explore six muscles on the front and
inside of the thigh!
Watch the outline trace each muscle, follow the
arrows, and connect the shape to its name.
We will show where it is, how to
recognize it, what movement it helps produce, and
what its name means.
Same muscle, different pictures.
Let's get started!
This is the rectus femoris, one of the
four quadriceps muscles on the front of your
thigh.
It runs from the front of your pelvis
toward your kneecap.
To identify it, look for the long, central
muscle running mostly straight down the front of
the thigh.
It helps straighten your knee and lift your
thigh at the hip.
“Rectus” means straight, and “femoris” means of the
thigh.
Your memory cue: straight down the front of
the thigh—rectus femoris.
This is the vastus lateralis, a large quadriceps
muscle on the outside of your thigh.
Look for the broad muscle along the outer
edge of the front thigh, extending toward the
knee.
It helps straighten your knee, like when you
kick your lower leg forward.
“Vastus” means large, and “lateralis” means toward the
side, away from the body’s midline.
Your memory cue: the large muscle on the
outside—vastus lateralis.
This is the vastus medialis, a quadriceps muscle
on the inner side of the front thigh.
Its easiest landmark is the teardrop-shaped bulge just
above the inside of your knee.
It helps straighten your knee.
“Vastus” means large, and “medialis” means toward the
body’s midline—the imaginary line dividing your body into
left and right halves.
Your memory cue: inner knee, teardrop shape—vastus medialis.
This is the vastus intermedius, a deep quadriceps
muscle on the front of your thigh, close
to the thigh bone.
To identify it, check the layer: it becomes
visible when the muscle covering the center of
the front thigh is lifted away.
It helps straighten your knee.
“Vastus” means large, and “intermedius” means in between,
describing its position between the inner and outer
quadriceps muscles.
Your memory cue: deep in the middle—vastus intermedius.
This is the sartorius, a long, narrow muscle
crossing the front of your thigh.
Follow its diagonal path from the outer front
of your hip to the inner side of
your shin, just below the knee.
That diagonal strap is its identifying feature.
It helps lift your thigh, move and turn
it outward, and bend your knee—movements used when
sitting cross-legged.
Its name comes from the Latin word for
tailor, associated with that sitting position.
Your memory cue: the diagonal seat belt—sartorius.
This is the gracilis, a long, slender muscle
along the inside of your thigh.
It runs from the lower pelvis to the
inner shin, just below the knee.
To identify it, look for a narrow strap
following the inner edge of the thigh, with
a mostly vertical course.
It helps pull your thigh inward toward your
other leg and bend your knee.
“Gracilis” means slender.
Your memory cue: the slender inner-thigh strap—gracilis.
This is the occipitofrontalis.
You'll find it across the scalp, with a
front forehead belly and a back-of-head belly.
To identify it, look for two muscular ends
joined by a broad sheet over the skull.
It moves the scalp; its front belly raises
the eyebrows.
occipito means back of head.
frontalis means forehead.
Your memory cue: Front and back, joined across
the cap.
This is the frontalis.
You'll find it on the forehead, extending upward
from the eyebrows.
To identify it, find the thin, broad muscle
directly above the eyebrows.
It raises the eyebrows and makes horizontal forehead
wrinkles.
frontalis means of the forehead.
Your memory cue: Front of the head, eyebrows
up.
This is the occipitalis.
You'll find it at the back of the
scalp, above the upper neck.
To identify it, find the short muscle belly
behind the ear toward the back of the
skull.
It pulls the scalp backward.
occipitalis means of the back of the head.
Your memory cue: Occipitalis pulls the cap back.
This is the epicranial aponeurosis.
You'll find it over the top of the
skull, connecting the front and back scalp muscles.
To identify it, identify the broad, pale sheet
between the scalp muscle bellies.
It transmits the pull between scalp muscles; it
does not contract itself.
epi means upon.
cranial means skull.
aponeurosis means broad tendon sheet.
Your memory cue: The scalp's white connecting cap.
This is the corrugator supercilii.
You'll find it at the inner end of
each eyebrow, near the bridge of the nose.
To identify it, look for a small, short
muscle beneath the inner eyebrow, not the whole
ring around the eye.
It draws the eyebrows inward and downward, making
vertical frown lines.
corrugator means wrinkler.
supercilii means of the eyebrow.
Your memory cue: Corrugator creases the brows together.
This is the orbicularis oculi.
You'll find it encircling the eye opening and
eyelids.
To identify it, follow the circular muscle around
the eye socket.
It closes the eyelids, as in blinking or
squeezing the eyes shut.
orbicularis means circular.
oculi means of the eye.
Your memory cue: Oculi closes the eye.
This is the nasalis.
You'll find it over the bridge and sides
of the nose.
To identify it, find the small muscle spread
across the nasal cartilages, above the nostrils.
It helps compress or widen the nostril openings,
depending on its part.
nasalis means of the nose.
Your memory cue: Nasalis names the nose.
This is the procerus.
You'll find it at the root of the
nose, between the eyebrows.
To identify it, look for the small vertical
patch over the upper bridge of the nose.
It pulls the inner eyebrow region downward and
wrinkles the bridge of the nose.
procerus means elongated.
Your memory cue: A little vertical strip over
the nose bridge.
This is the buccinator.
You'll find it deep in the cheek, forming
the muscular wall beside the teeth.
To identify it, find the broad cheek sheet
running toward the corner of the mouth.
It presses the cheek against the teeth, helping
keep food between them and assisting blowing.
buccinator means trumpeter.
Your memory cue: The trumpeter squeezes the cheek.
This is the risorius.
You'll find it a thin superficial band running
horizontally toward the corner of the mouth.
To identify it, look for a narrow sideways
strap rather than a diagonal cheek muscle.
It pulls the mouth corner laterally, widening the
mouth.
risorius means laughing.
Your memory cue: Risorius pulls the corner sideways.
This is the zygomaticus major.
You'll find it from the cheekbone diagonally down
to the corner of the mouth.
To identify it, find the larger diagonal smile
strap ending at the mouth corner.
It lifts the mouth corner upward and outward.
zygomaticus means of the cheekbone.
major means larger.
Your memory cue: Major moves the mouth corner
into a smile.
This is the zygomaticus minor.
You'll find it from the cheekbone to the
upper lip, medial to the larger smile strap.
To identify it, look for the smaller diagonal
strip reaching the upper lip.
It raises the upper lip.
zygomaticus means of the cheekbone.
minor means smaller.
Your memory cue: Minor lifts the lip; major
lifts the corner.
This is the orbicularis oris.
You'll find it encircling the mouth within the
lips.
To identify it, trace the circular muscle surrounding
the mouth opening.
It closes and purses the lips, as for
kissing or whistling.
orbicularis means circular.
oris means of the mouth.
Your memory cue: Oris makes the mouth ring.
This is the depressor anguli oris.
You'll find it below and lateral to the
mouth, extending from the lower jaw to the
mouth corner.
To identify it, find the triangular muscle whose
upper point reaches the corner of the mouth.
It pulls the mouth corner downward, helping form
a frown.
depressor means lowers.
anguli means of the angle.
oris means of the mouth.
Your memory cue: Depress the angle: corner down.
This is the depressor labii inferioris.
You'll find it below the lower lip, closer
to the center than the mouth-corner depressor.
To identify it, look for the short band
entering the lower lip rather than the mouth
corner.
It pulls the lower lip downward and slightly
outward.
depressor means lowers.
labii means of the lip.
inferioris means lower.
Your memory cue: Inferior lip goes down.
This is the levator labii superioris.
You'll find it alongside the nose, descending toward
the upper lip.
To identify it, find the vertical strip from
below the eye toward the upper lip beside
the nose.
It raises the upper lip.
levator means lifter.
labii means of the lip.
superioris means upper.
Your memory cue: Superior lip goes up.
This is the mentalis.
You'll find it at the center of the
chin, immediately below the lower lip.
To identify it, find the small paired muscle
bellies near the chin's midline.
It raises and protrudes the lower lip and
wrinkles the chin.
mentalis means of the chin.
Your memory cue: Mentalis makes the pout.
This is the masseter.
You'll find it on the outside of the
jaw, from the cheekbone arch to the angle
of the lower jaw.
To identify it, find the thick rectangular jaw
muscle just in front of the ear.
It powerfully closes the jaw by raising the
lower jaw.
masseter means chewer.
Your memory cue: Masseter is the mighty jaw
closer.
This is the temporalis.
You'll find it on the side of the
skull above the ear.
To identify it, look for a broad fan
converging downward toward the lower jaw.
It closes the jaw and helps pull it
backward.
temporalis means of the temple.
Your memory cue: The temple fan closes and
retracts.
This is the lateral pterygoid.
You'll find it deep behind the cheek, running
mostly horizontally toward the jaw joint.
To identify it, look for the short horizontal
muscle reaching the front of the jaw-joint region.
It helps open and protrude the jaw and
move it side to side.
lateral means toward the side.
pterygoid means wing-shaped region.
Your memory cue: Lateral lies sideways and helps
the jaw slide.
This is the medial pterygoid.
You'll find it deep on the inside of
the lower jaw near its angle.
To identify it, find the deep muscle running
down toward the inner surface of the jaw
angle.
It raises and protrudes the jaw.
medial means toward the midline.
pterygoid means wing-shaped region.
Your memory cue: Medial is the inside jaw
closer.
This is the digastric.
You'll find it beneath the jaw, with two
bellies connected by an intermediate tendon near the
hyoid.
To identify it, trace two muscular segments forming
a bent sling under the jaw.
It helps open the jaw and raise the
hyoid during swallowing.
di means two.
gastric means bellies.
Your memory cue: Digastric: two bellies, one sling.
This is the anterior belly of digastric.
You'll find it under the front of the
jaw, running from the inner chin toward the
hyoid.
To identify it, find the forward belly of
the two-belly sling, closest to the chin.
It helps lower the jaw and raise the
hyoid.
anterior means front.
digastric means two bellies.
Your memory cue: Anterior belly aims toward the
chin.
This is the posterior belly of digastric.
You'll find it under the back of the
jaw, descending from behind the ear toward the
hyoid.
To identify it, find the rear belly of
the two-belly sling, closest to the mastoid region.
It helps raise and retract the hyoid during
swallowing.
posterior means back.
digastric means two bellies.
Your memory cue: Posterior belly points behind the
ear.
This is the mylohyoid.
You'll find it across the floor of the
mouth, between the inner lower jaw and the
hyoid.
To identify it, look for a broad sheet
forming a hammock beneath the tongue.
It raises the floor of the mouth and
the hyoid.
mylo means molar region.
hyoid means hyoid bone.
Your memory cue: Mylohyoid is the mouth-floor hammock.
This is the stylohyoid.
You'll find it a slender strip from the
skull just behind the ear toward the hyoid.
To identify it, find the thin muscle alongside
the posterior digastric belly; its tendon may split
around the digastric tendon.
It raises and retracts the hyoid during swallowing.
stylo means styloid process.
hyoid means hyoid bone.
Your memory cue: Stylohyoid is the slender skull-to-hyoid
string.
This is the sternocleidomastoid.
You'll find it along each side of the
neck, from the upper chest and collarbone to
the skull behind the ear.
To identify it, find the prominent oblique strap
with two lower attachments.
One side turns the face to the opposite
side; both sides help flex the neck.
sterno means sternum.
cleido means clavicle.
mastoid means skull attachment.
Your memory cue: Chest, collarbone, behind the ear:
three attachments in one name.
This is the omohyoid.
You'll find it a thin strap crossing the
lower neck from the shoulder blade toward the
hyoid.
To identify it, trace two narrow bellies with
an intermediate tendon, crossing the lower side of
the neck.
It depresses and stabilizes the hyoid.
omo means shoulder.
hyoid means hyoid bone.
Your memory cue: Omo starts at the shoulder.
This is the platysma.
You'll find it immediately beneath the skin over
the front and sides of the neck.
To identify it, look for a very thin,
wide surface sheet rather than a rounded strap.
It tenses the neck skin and helps draw
the lower lip and mouth corner downward.
platys means broad or flat.
Your memory cue: Platysma is the flat neck
sheet.
This is the levator scapulae.
You'll find it from the upper neck to
the upper inner corner of the shoulder blade.
To identify it, find the narrow strap descending
to the superior angle of the scapula.
It raises the shoulder blade and helps rotate
it downward.
levator means lifter.
scapulae means of the shoulder blade.
Your memory cue: Levator lifts the shoulder blade.
This is the rhomboideus major.
You'll find it between the upper back spine
and the inner edge of the shoulder blade,
below the scapular spine.
To identify it, find the larger oblique band
deep to trapezius, below the smaller rhomboid.
It pulls the shoulder blade toward the spine
and holds it against the ribs.
rhomboideus means rhombus-shaped.
major means larger.
Your memory cue: Major is the larger, lower
rhomboid.
This is the rhomboideus minor.
You'll find it between the lower neck spine
and the inner end of the shoulder-blade spine.
To identify it, find the small band immediately
above the larger rhomboid.
It retracts and stabilizes the shoulder blade.
rhomboideus means rhombus-shaped.
minor means smaller.
Your memory cue: Minor is the smaller, higher
rhomboid.
This is the pectoralis minor.
You'll find it deep in the front chest,
from upper ribs to the hook-like process of
the shoulder blade.
To identify it, find a small triangular muscle
under the broad chest muscle, converging toward the
front of the shoulder.
It draws the shoulder blade forward and downward
and helps stabilize it.
pectoralis means of the chest.
minor means smaller.
Your memory cue: Minor is the small, deep
chest triangle.
This is the serratus anterior.
You'll find it along the side of the
ribs, wrapping toward the inner surface of the
shoulder blade.
To identify it, look for sawtooth-like slips interlocking
along the lateral ribs.
It pulls the shoulder blade forward and holds
it against the chest wall.
serratus means saw-toothed.
anterior means front.
Your memory cue: The boxer's sawteeth push the
shoulder blade forward.
This is the trapezius.
You'll find it superficially across the upper back
and back of the neck.
To identify it, find the large sheet extending
from the midline toward the shoulder blade; both
sides form a broad kite.
Different fibers raise, retract, lower, and upwardly rotate
the shoulder blade.
trapezius means trapezoid-shaped.
Your memory cue: The broad back kite positions
the shoulder blade.
This is the external abdominal oblique.
You'll find it the superficial muscle sheet along
the sides of the abdomen.
To identify it, look for fibers slanting downward
and toward the midline, like hands entering front
pockets.
It compresses the abdomen, flexes the trunk, and
rotates it toward the opposite side.
external means outer.
oblique means slanting.
Your memory cue: External fibers follow the hands-in-pockets
direction.
This is the internal abdominal oblique.
You'll find it in the side abdominal wall,
deep to the external oblique.
To identify it, look for the middle layer
with many fibers sloping upward and inward.
It compresses the abdomen and rotates the trunk
toward the same side.
internal means inner.
oblique means slanting.
Your memory cue: Internal inclines up and in.
This is the transverse abdominis.
You'll find it the deepest of the three
flat muscle layers in the side abdominal wall.
To identify it, find fibers traveling horizontally around
the abdomen, like a belt.
It compresses and supports the abdominal contents.
transverse means across.
abdominis means of the abdomen.
Your memory cue: Transverse tightens the waist belt.
This is the rectus abdominis.
You'll find it vertically along the front abdomen,
one muscle on each side of the midline.
To identify it, find the straight segmented strips
commonly called the six-pack.
It flexes the trunk and compresses the abdomen.
rectus means straight.
abdominis means of the abdomen.
Your memory cue: Rectus runs straight down the
abdomen.
This is the linea alba.
You'll find it down the midline of the
abdomen, between the paired rectus muscles.
To identify it, look for the pale vertical
seam joining the abdominal tendon sheets.
It connects the abdominal wall across the midline;
it does not actively contract.
linea means line.
alba means white.
Your memory cue: Linea alba is the white
center line.
This is the inguinal ligament.
You'll find it across the groin, from the
front hip prominence toward the pubic region.
To identify it, find the firm lower border
of the external oblique tendon sheet above the
upper thigh.
It forms a supporting boundary over structures passing
from the abdomen into the thigh.
inguinal means of the groin.
ligament means connecting band.
Your memory cue: Inguinal is the groin's firm
border.
This is the quadratus lumborum.
You'll find it deep in the lower back,
between the top of the pelvis and the
lowest rib.
To identify it, find the roughly rectangular muscle
lateral to the lumbar spine on the posterior
abdominal wall.
It bends the trunk to the same side
and stabilizes the lowest rib.
quadratus means square.
lumborum means of the loins.
Your memory cue: The square of the low
back.
This is the erector spinae.
You'll find it long muscle columns on both
sides of the spine, from the low back
upward.
To identify it, recognize the combined three-column mass
rather than one isolated slip.
It extends and laterally bends the spine and
helps maintain upright posture.
erector means one that raises.
spinae means of the spine.
Your memory cue: Erector spinae keeps the spine
erect.
This is the iliocostalis.
You'll find it the outermost column of the
erector-spinae group, running toward the ribs.
To identify it, find the most lateral back-extensor
column with rib attachments.
It helps extend and bend the spine to
the same side.
ilio means ilium.
costalis means of the ribs.
Your memory cue: Iliocostalis is the outside rib
column.
This is the longissimus.
You'll find it the middle column of the
erector-spinae group along the back.
To identify it, find the long central column
between the rib-side column and the column nearest
the spinous processes.
It helps extend the spine and bend it
to the same side.
longissimus means longest.
Your memory cue: Longissimus is the long middle
column.
This is the spinalis.
You'll find it the most medial erector-spinae column,
alongside the vertebral spinous processes.
To identify it, find the narrow column closest
to the bony midline of the back.
It helps extend the spine.
spinalis means of the spine.
Your memory cue: Spinalis stays beside the spinal
midline.
This is the coracobrachialis.
You'll find it on the inner upper arm,
running from the front shoulder-blade hook to the
humerus.
To identify it, look for a slender muscle
high on the medial upper arm, deep beside
the biceps.
It moves the upper arm forward and toward
the body.
coraco means coracoid process.
brachialis means of the arm.
Your memory cue: Coracoid to arm: coracobrachialis.
This is the deltoid.
You'll find it capping the shoulder and covering
the upper end of the humerus.
To identify it, look for the large triangular
shoulder cap.
It raises the arm to the side; front
and back fibers also move it forward or
backward.
deltoid means shaped like the Greek letter delta.
Your memory cue: Delta is the triangular shoulder
cap.
This is the latissimus dorsi.
You'll find it across the broad middle and
lower back, sweeping toward the upper arm.
To identify it, find the large sheet forming
much of the back edge of the armpit.
It pulls the arm backward, inward, and into
internal rotation.
latissimus means broadest.
dorsi means of the back.
Your memory cue: The broad back sheet pulls
the arm down and back.
This is the pectoralis major.
You'll find it superficially across the front chest,
converging on the upper arm.
To identify it, look for the large fan-shaped
chest muscle forming the front armpit fold.
It brings the arm forward, across the body,
and into internal rotation.
pectoralis means of the chest.
major means larger.
Your memory cue: Major is the big front-chest
fan.
This is the teres major.
You'll find it from the lower outer part
of the shoulder blade to the upper humerus.
To identify it, find the thicker rounded band
below teres minor, near the back armpit fold.
It pulls the arm inward and backward and
rotates it internally.
teres means rounded.
major means larger.
Your memory cue: Major pulls in; minor turns
out.
This is the supraspinatus.
You'll find it on the back of the
shoulder blade, above its prominent bony spine.
To identify it, find the small muscle filling
the shallow fossa above that ridge.
It helps begin arm abduction and stabilizes the
shoulder joint.
supra means above.
spinatus means relating to the scapular spine.
Your memory cue: Supra sits above the spine.
This is the infraspinatus.
You'll find it on the back of the
shoulder blade, below its bony spine.
To identify it, find the broad triangular muscle
filling the large hollow below the ridge.
It rotates the arm outward and stabilizes the
shoulder.
infra means below.
spinatus means relating to the scapular spine.
Your memory cue: Infra is the big triangle
below the spine.
This is the teres minor.
You'll find it along the outer border of
the shoulder blade, below the broad infraspinous region.
To identify it, find the small narrow rounded
band above the thicker teres major.
It rotates the upper arm outward and stabilizes
the shoulder.
teres means rounded.
minor means smaller.
Your memory cue: Minor is the smaller cuff
band that turns out.
This is the subscapularis.
You'll find it on the front, rib-facing surface
of the shoulder blade.
To identify it, turn the scapula toward its
rib-facing side and find the broad triangle filling
that surface.
It rotates the arm inward and stabilizes the
shoulder.
sub means under.
scapularis means of the shoulder blade.
Your memory cue: Subscapularis sits on the underside
facing the ribs.
This is the biceps brachii.
You'll find it superficially along the front of
the upper arm.
To identify it, find the prominent two-headed muscle
whose tendon continues toward the radius near the
elbow.
It bends the elbow and turns the forearm
palm-up.
bi means two.
ceps means heads.
brachii means of the arm.
Your memory cue: Two heads in front: biceps
brachii.
This is the brachialis.
You'll find it deep on the front of
the lower upper arm, beneath the biceps.
To identify it, find the broad muscle exposed
beside or under the biceps near the elbow.
It bends the elbow regardless of forearm rotation.
brachialis means of the arm.
Your memory cue: Brachialis is the deep elbow
bender.
This is the brachioradialis.
You'll find it on the lateral, thumb-side forearm,
starting above the elbow.
To identify it, find the large superficial band
forming the lateral border of the elbow pit.
It bends the elbow, especially with the thumb
pointing upward.
brachio means arm.
radialis means radius.
Your memory cue: Arm to radius, thumb-up elbow
bend.
This is the triceps brachii.
You'll find it across the back of the
upper arm, ending at the point of the
elbow.
To identify it, look for the large three-headed
posterior arm mass.
It straightens the elbow; the long head also
helps move the arm backward and inward.
tri means three.
ceps means heads.
brachii means of the arm.
Your memory cue: Three heads behind straighten the
elbow.
This is the flexor carpi ulnaris.
You'll find it along the little-finger side of
the anterior forearm.
To identify it, follow the superficial ulnar-edge muscle
toward the wrist on the pinky side.
It bends the wrist and moves the hand
toward the little-finger side.
flexor means bender.
carpi means of the wrist.
ulnaris means ulna side.
Your memory cue: Flex the wrist toward the
pinky.
This is the flexor carpi radialis.
You'll find it on the anterior forearm toward
the thumb-side wrist.
To identify it, follow its long tendon toward
the base of the hand on the radial
side.
It bends the wrist and moves the hand
toward the thumb side.
flexor means bender.
carpi means of the wrist.
radialis means radius side.
Your memory cue: Flex the wrist toward the
thumb.
This is the palmaris longus.
You'll find it superficially in the middle of
the anterior forearm, with a long tendon toward
the palm.
To identify it, find a small proximal belly
and a slender central tendon entering the palm's
connective sheet.
It tenses the palm's connective tissue and weakly
helps flex the wrist.
palmaris means of the palm.
longus means long.
Your memory cue: A long central string to
the palm.
This is the pronator teres.
You'll find it across the upper anterior forearm,
running obliquely from the inner elbow toward the
radius.
To identify it, look for the short diagonal
band near the elbow rather than a long
wrist tendon.
It turns the forearm palm-down.
pronator means palm-down rotator.
teres means rounded.
Your memory cue: Pronator turns the palm toward
the floor.
This is the flexor digitorum superficialis.
You'll find it in the anterior forearm, forming
a finger-flexor layer above the deepest flexors.
To identify it, trace a broad belly dividing
into four tendons for the four fingers.
It bends the middle finger joints and helps
bend the wrist.
flexor means bender.
digitorum means of the digits.
superficialis means nearer the surface.
Your memory cue: Superficial fingers bend at the
middle joints.
This is the flexor digitorum profundus.
You'll find it deep in the anterior forearm,
toward the ulna.
To identify it, find the deep finger-flexor mass
with four tendons continuing to the fingertips.
It bends the distal joints of the four
fingers.
flexor means bender.
digitorum means of the digits.
profundus means deep.
Your memory cue: Profundus goes deep and reaches
the fingertips.
This is the flexor pollicis longus.
You'll find it deep in the anterior forearm
on the thumb side.
To identify it, follow the single long tendon
heading to the thumb rather than four finger
tendons.
It bends the thumb, including its end joint.
flexor means bender.
pollicis means of the thumb.
longus means long.
Your memory cue: One long flexor for one
thumb.
This is the supinator.
You'll find it deep around the upper radius,
just below the lateral elbow.
To identify it, find the short muscle wrapping
around the proximal radius.
It turns the forearm palm-up.
supinator means palm-up rotator.
Your memory cue: Hold a bowl of soup:
supination turns the palm up.
This is the extensor carpi radialis longus.
You'll find it along the thumb-side posterior forearm,
with a relatively long proximal belly.
To identify it, trace the more lateral radial
wrist extensor toward the base of the second
metacarpal.

It straightens the wrist and moves it toward
the thumb side.
extensor means straightener.
carpi means wrist.
radialis means radius side.

the posterior forearm.

a tendon heading to the fifth metacarpal.
It straightens the wrist and moves the hand
toward the pinky side.
extensor means straightener.
carpi means wrist.
ulnaris means ulna side.
Your memory cue: Ulnaris extends toward the pinky.
This is the extensor digitorum.
You'll find it superficially in the center of
the posterior forearm.
To identify it, look for a broad muscle
splitting into four tendons across the back of
the hand.
It straightens the four fingers and helps extend
the wrist.
extensor means straightener.
digitorum means of the digits.
Your memory cue: One central muscle, four finger
tendons.
This is the extensor digiti minimi.
You'll find it a narrow strip in the
posterior forearm on the little-finger side of the
common finger extensor.

to the fifth finger.
It straightens the little finger.
extensor means straightener.
digiti means of the digit.
minimi means smallest.
Your memory cue: Minimi means the smallest finger.
This is the extensor indicis.
You'll find it deep in the distal posterior
forearm near the ulna.
To identify it, find the small deep muscle
with a single tendon joining the index-finger extensor
tendon.
It straightens the index finger.
extensor means straightener.
indicis means of the index finger.
Your memory cue: Indicis points to the index.
This is the abductor pollicis longus.
You'll find it deep in the posterior forearm,
crossing toward the thumb side of the wrist.
To identify it, follow its tendon toward the
base of the thumb metacarpal.
It moves the thumb away from the hand
at its base.
abductor means moves away.
pollicis means thumb.
longus means long.
Your memory cue: Abductor carries the thumb away.
This is the extensor pollicis brevis.
You'll find it on the deep posterior forearm,
traveling toward the thumb-side wrist.
To identify it, trace the short thumb extensor
to the base of the thumb's proximal phalanx.
It straightens the thumb at its knuckle.
extensor means straightener.
pollicis means thumb.
brevis means short.
Your memory cue: Brevis stops at the nearer
thumb bone.
This is the extensor pollicis longus.
You'll find it deep in the posterior forearm,
with a tendon angling across the back of
the wrist toward the thumb.
To identify it, follow the long oblique tendon
to the distal thumb phalanx.
It straightens the thumb, especially its end joint.
extensor means straightener.
pollicis means thumb.
longus means long.
Your memory cue: Longus goes all the way
to the thumb tip.
This is the gluteus maximus.
You'll find it superficially across the buttock.
To identify it, find the largest, outermost gluteal

It extends and outwardly rotates the hip, as
when rising from a chair.
gluteus means buttock.
maximus means largest.
Your memory cue: Maximus is the big surface
power muscle.
This is the gluteus medius.
You'll find it on the outer hip, deep
to the large superficial buttock muscle.
To identify it, find a broad fan from
the side of the pelvis toward the upper
outer femur.
It moves the thigh sideways and stabilizes the
pelvis during single-leg stance.
gluteus means buttock.
medius means middle.
Your memory cue: Medius is the middle fan
that steadies the pelvis.
This is the gluteus minimus.
You'll find it deep on the outer hip,
beneath the middle gluteal layer.
To identify it, look for the smallest, deepest
gluteal fan against the outer pelvis.
It abducts and inwardly rotates the thigh.
gluteus means buttock.
minimus means smallest.
Your memory cue: Minimus: smallest and deepest.
This is the tensor fascia latae.
You'll find it at the front outer corner

broad fibrous band.

at the top of the long outer-thigh band.

abduct, and inwardly rotate the hip.
tensor means tightener.
fascia lata means broad thigh fascia.
Your memory cue: The tensor tightens the outer-thigh
band.
This is the iliotibial band.
You'll find it a long, thick connective-tissue strip

continuing from the hip toward the outer knee.
It transmits muscle tension and helps stabilize the
lateral hip and knee.
ilio means ilium.
tibial means tibia.
band means strip.
Your memory cue: IT is the outside thigh's
tough track.
This is the iliopsoas.
You'll find it at the front of the
hip, where two deep muscles converge toward the
upper femur.

crossing in front of the hip joint.
It strongly lifts the thigh at the hip.
ilio means ilium.
psoas means loin region.
Your memory cue: Iliacus plus psoas makes iliopsoas.
This is the iliacus.
You'll find it inside the pelvic bowl, filling
the broad inner surface of the ilium.

spread across the iliac fossa.
It helps lift the thigh at the hip.
iliacus means of the ilium.
Your memory cue: Iliacus fills the iliac bowl.
This is the psoas major.
You'll find it alongside the lumbar spine, descending
over the pelvic brim toward the upper femur.

flexor next to the lower spinal column.
It flexes the hip and helps flex the
trunk when the lower limb is fixed.
psoas means loin region.
major means larger.
Your memory cue: Psoas is the long strip
from the low back to the hip.
This is the piriformis.
You'll find it deep in the buttock, from
the sacrum toward the outer upper femur.

a flexed thigh.
piri means pear.
formis means shaped.
Your memory cue: Pear above the deep-rotator stack.
This is the superior gemellus.

above the tendon that bends out of the

the hip.
superior means upper.
gemellus means little twin.
Your memory cue: The upper twin sits above
the tendon.
This is the obturator internus.
You'll find it on the inside of the
pelvic wall, with its tendon turning out toward
the back of the hip.

the two small gemellus muscles.
It turns the thigh outward and helps stabilize
the hip.
obturator means obturator opening.
internus means inner.
Your memory cue: Internus turns from inside the
pelvis, between the twins.
This is the inferior gemellus.
You'll find it deep behind the hip, immediately
below the obturator-internus tendon.
To identify it, find the lower small muscle
hugging that tendon.
It helps turn the thigh outward and stabilize
the hip.
inferior means lower.
gemellus means little twin.
Your memory cue: The lower twin sits below
the tendon.
This is the quadratus femoris.
You'll find it deep behind the hip, below

femur.

quadratus means square.
femoris means of the thigh.
Your memory cue: The square sits at the
bottom of the deep stack.
This is the pectineus.
You'll find it high in the inner front
thigh, just below the groin.

pectineus means comb-like.
Your memory cue: The little comb sits high

This is the adductor brevis.

adductor means draws toward.
brevis means short.
Your memory cue: Brevis is the short, deep

This is the adductor longus.

thigh, from the pubic region toward the middle

adductor means draws toward.
longus means long.
Your memory cue: Longus is the long front-medial

adductor means draws toward.
magnus means great or large.

ceps means heads.
femoris means of the thigh.

semi means half.
membranosus means membranous.

brevis means short.

calcaneus means heel bone.

This is the popliteus.
You'll find it deep across the back of
the knee, just below the joint.

This is the tibialis posterior.

You'll find it deep on the tibial side

digitorum means digits.
longus means long.
Your memory cue: Four deep tendons curl the

You'll find it deep on the fibular side

hallucis means big toe.
longus means long.
Your memory cue: The big-toe flexor powers the
push-off.
